## Preface

[Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/) is a cloud-based platform hosted by [Google](https://www.google.com/) that uses Google’s high-performance and intrinsically parallel computing system to subdivide computations across Google's computational infrastructure, accelerating computational processes (Gorelick et al., 2017). The platform has been primarily designed to process and analyze satellite imagery and geospatial datasets, making computationally demanding workflows more accessible for research, education, and other non-profit uses at no user cost.

Up until 2008, using satellite imagery for data analysis was expensive. In 2008, however, the United States Geological Survey ([USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/)) opted for a free and open access policy on the use of the most popular satellite platform at the time - Landsat (Woodcock et al., 2008). The release of the Landsat catalog for free use by the public opened enormous possibilities to expand earth observation research (Woulder et al., 2019). However, with so much data available to the user community, the limitation shifted from data collection to data processing.

Personal computers are generally limited in computational power to analyze the amount of data that a composite of Landsat images require. Data storage is also limited. Supercomputers can be used for this purpose, but access to supercomputers is only an option for researchers working in certain institutions. [Google](https://www.google.com/) opened the option for all users with internet access to operate on high computing infrastructure through the new platform, [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/).

When satellite data accessibility is combined with free access to fast computing processes, researchers and students have the possibility to carry out computationally demanding projects in a matter of hours or minutes. For ecologists, this has opened the horizons of research possibilities in unthinkable ways. And while a lot of attention
has been put into the use of [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/) for remote sensing scientists (Tamimina et al., 2020), the tool has not reached the
spatial ecological field in its full capacity. In this tutorial, we explore different applications that this platform provides to analyze data for projects focused on spatial ecology.

### Goals
This workshop is intended to provide an introduction to [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/) for participants in the fields of ecology, conservation, and wildlife biology. The course will begin by covering the basics of [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/) and JavaScript coding before moving on to spatial data manipulation and analyses. Participants need no prior experience working with [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/), but should have a basic understanding of Geographic Information System (GIS) data and concepts, such as raster (including stacks or multi-band images), vectors, projections, and spatial resolution. This course is a continuation of a previous year’s module “Introduction to Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and Wildlife Population Monitoring in R.” 

At the conclusion of the course, we will combine [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/) workflows with population analysis in [R](https://cran.r-project.org/), with a goal of creating a community of practice that have the skills necessary to expand upon science-based monitoring of wildlife populations across Kenya.

### Learning Outcomes

You are expected to use your own computer for all exercises. By the end of this course, you will be able to:

 * Understand [GEE's](https://earthengine.google.com/) web interface
 * Access and manipulate spatial data from the [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/) catalog
 * Understand the fundamentals of JavaScript code
 * Perform basic spatial data processing (i.e., standard GIS operations)
 * Gain experience with species distribution modeling (i.e., random forest)
 * Download [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/) data to incorporate in [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) workflows to assess species abundance
 * Use [R](https://cran.r-project.org/) to create maps and visualize data
 * Make maps that show predictions based on statistical models

### How to use this material

Here we present a tutorial that will guide you on the use of different modeling techniques for data analysis. The main goal of this tutorial is to provide the foundational building blocks for you to master your skills to analyze your own data using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/).

The tutorial is organized in 4 main sections. Section 1 is an introduction to [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/) and the JavaScript language we use
to code. Section 2 will guide you on how to manage data, such as images and geometries, in [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/). Section 3 illustrations how to export data from [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/) to other interfaces like [R](https://cran.r-project.org/), with a focus on making visualizations of your data. And finally, we will end with Section 4 and provide an introduction to implementing Species Distribution Models in [GEE](https://earthengine.google.com/). 

> All the code used in these exercises is available [here](https://code.earthengine.google.com/?accept_repo=users/jaredstabach/NASA_EcoCons_Mara).
